# Day 37: The two-move match

## Prerequisites

*   [Day 36](https://hardware.ellietaghavi.com/llm/day-36.md) (Smith chart navigation).

## Introduction & background

Impedance matching ensures maximum power transfer and minimal reflections between stages in an RF circuit. By using an "L-match" network (a combination of one series reactive element and one shunt reactive element, typically a capacitor and inductor), you can navigate from almost any starting impedance on the Smith chart to the exact center (a perfect 50 Ω match). The first element (shunt or series) moves you along a constant conductance or resistance circle until you intersect the circle passing through the center, and the second element brings you perfectly home.

## Core equations

Quality Factor (Q) cost of a matching network:
$$Q \approx \frac{f_c}{BW}$$

## Diagram

[Antenna-Theory: Impedance Matching with Smith Charts](http://www.antenna-theory.com/tutorial/smith/smithchart5.php)

## What you're building

1. A simulated L-match network on a Smith chart to transform a $Z = 20 - j35 \ \Omega$ load to 50 Ω at 433 MHz.
2. A verification script in `scikit-rf` to plot the resulting $S_{11}$ dip and verify the bandwidth.
3. An independent matching design for a second load of $Z = 80 + j20 \ \Omega$.

## Activity

On the chart, match Z = 20 − j35 Ω to 50 Ω at 433 MHz with an L-match: one shunt move onto the circle through the center, one series move home. Extract the L and C values. Verify the S11 dip in scikit-rf. Then repeat, solo, for Z = 80 + j20 Ω.

## Question to answer

1. Why do exactly two elements suffice for (almost) any load?
2. What did your match's Q cost in bandwidth (sweep ±50 MHz and look)?
